questions.explanation: Wegener's 1912 drift hypothesis was rejected for lacking a mechanism. Seafloor spreading evidence (magnetic stripes, age gradient) confirmed mantle convection drives plates. One theory unified previously disparate phenomena: a hallmark of good science.

questions.prompt: The philosophical shock of deep time was that it:
options: Undermined teleological worldviews — humans are recent, late, and contingent
questions.correctAnswer: Undermined teleological worldviews — humans are recent, late, and contingent
questions.explanation: 4.5 billion years vs. 6,000. Humans are ~0.004% of Earth history. Mass extinctions removed 90%+ of species without apparent purpose. Influenced Nietzsche, existentialism, process philosophy, and ushered in modern naturalism.

questions.prompt: Stromatolites (3.5+ billion years old) tell us that:
options: Cyanobacteria oxygenated the atmosphere via photosynthesis
questions.correctAnswer: Cyanobacteria oxygenated the atmosphere via photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Microbial mats trapping sediment. Cyanobacteria split water and emit O2 as waste. The Great Oxidation Event ~2.4 Bya is recorded in banded iron formations. Atmospheric oxygen enabled aerobic life and the ozone shield.

questions.prompt: The Anthropocene as a proposed geological epoch is debated because:
options: The geological record is too short
Choosing a single globally synchronous boundary marker (golden spike) is hard
questions.correctAnswer: Choosing a single globally synchronous boundary marker (golden spike) is hard
questions.explanation: Candidates: 1610 CO2 dip from the Columbian exchange; the Industrial Revolution; 1950 nuclear fallout (most preferred). Stratigraphers want a globally synchronous, well-preserved horizon. The decision is geological and philosophical.

questions.prompt: The 'rare Earth hypothesis' claims that:
options: Complex life requires an improbable confluence (plate tectonics, moon, magnetic field, Jupiter, etc.) sustained over billions of years
Only Earth has any life by definition
questions.correctAnswer: Complex life requires an improbable confluence (plate tectonics, moon, magnetic field, Jupiter, etc.) sustained over billions of years
questions.explanation: Bacteria might be common; multicellular animals may be rare. Plate tectonics regulates the carbon-cycle thermostat. The magnetic field shields the atmosphere. Jupiter clears asteroids. Each factor depends on specific geology — astronomy + biology + philosophy of life.

title: Alchemy to Chemistry
description: Phlogiston, atomism, and the periodic table — how chemistry shed mysticism and what it kept.

questions.prompt: Alchemists sought to transmute base metals into gold. Modern view: this IS possible via:
questions.correctAnswer: Nuclear reactions (changing proton number)
questions.explanation: Chemistry rearranges electrons; nuclei stay fixed. Gold (Z=79) requires changing proton count, which is the nuclear domain. Particle accelerators have made tiny amounts. Alchemists' goal was right; their methods were the wrong domain.

questions.prompt: Phlogiston theory said burning released a substance called phlogiston. Lavoisier killed it by:
options: Showing combustion increases mass — oxygen is consumed, not phlogiston released
questions.correctAnswer: Showing combustion increases mass — oxygen is consumed, not phlogiston released
questions.explanation: Careful weighing showed metals gain mass when calcined. Phlogiston theorists posited 'negative weight' to save the theory. Lavoisier identified oxygen as the consumed gas. Quantitative method killed qualitative theory and gave birth to modern chemistry.

questions.prompt: Dalton (1803) revived atomism. His core empirical argument was:
options: Laws of definite and multiple proportions are explained if matter consists of discrete atoms with fixed masses
questions.correctAnswer: Laws of definite and multiple proportions are explained if matter consists of discrete atoms with fixed masses
questions.explanation: Compounds combine in fixed ratios (water is always H:O = 1:8 by mass). Multiple compounds of the same elements show small-integer mass ratios. These patterns demand discrete units. An empirical resurrection of Democritus.

questions.prompt: Why was atomism philosophically threatening for centuries?
options: It implied materialism: the world reducible to particles and void, with no inherent purpose
questions.correctAnswer: It implied materialism: the world reducible to particles and void, with no inherent purpose
questions.explanation: Aristotelian physics treated matter as substance plus form. Atomism (Democritus, Epicurus, Lucretius) reduced the cosmos to blind collisions. The Church rejected it for centuries. Galileo, Boyle, and Newton revived it cautiously. Implications still debated in metaphysics.

questions.prompt: Mendeleev's periodic table (1869) won credibility because he:
options: Was the first to attempt a table
Predicted properties of undiscovered elements (Ga, Sc, Ge) and was right
questions.correctAnswer: Predicted properties of undiscovered elements (Ga, Sc, Ge) and was right
questions.explanation: He left gaps where the pattern demanded missing elements. When gallium (1875) and scandium (1879) were discovered with predicted properties, the table won credibility. Risky predictions vindicated — a Popperian gold standard.

questions.prompt: Why does the periodic table work? Quantum mechanical answer:
options: Electron orbitals fill in patterns; valence shell configuration determines chemistry
questions.correctAnswer: Electron orbitals fill in patterns; valence shell configuration determines chemistry
questions.explanation: Schrodinger equation plus Pauli exclusion gives s, p, d, f orbitals. Period lengths 2, 8, 18, 32 = sum of 2(2L+1). Mendeleev did not know this; the table predicted the physics rather than the other way around. An empirical pattern revealing deep theory.

questions.prompt: Vitalism held that organic compounds required a 'life force' to make. What killed it?
options: Wohler synthesizing urea (1828) from ammonium cyanate — inorganic precursors yielding an organic product
questions.correctAnswer: Wohler synthesizing urea (1828) from ammonium cyanate — inorganic precursors yielding an organic product
questions.explanation: Urea is biological (from urine). Wohler made it from ammonium cyanate, with no living input. A bridge between organic and inorganic. Vitalism slowly collapsed; biochemistry emerged. Life is special chemistry, not a special substance.

questions.prompt: Mach and Ostwald (~1900) attacked atomic theory on philosophical grounds, arguing:
options: Atoms are unobservable theoretical entities; only observable phenomena are scientific
questions.correctAnswer: Atoms are unobservable theoretical entities; only observable phenomena are scientific
questions.explanation: Positivist/instrumentalist view: science should describe observables, not posit hidden things. Einstein's 1905 Brownian motion paper made atoms quantitatively required. Perrin's 1908 experiments clinched it. Realism vs. instrumentalism debates persist in philosophy of science.

questions.prompt: The Haber-Bosch process (1909-1913) was civilization-changing because it:
questions.correctAnswer: Enabled synthetic fertilizer, feeding billions
questions.explanation: Roughly 50% of nitrogen in human bodies today passed through Haber-Bosch. Without it, world population plateaus around 4 billion. It also enabled WWI explosives. One reaction reshapes population, agriculture, and geopolitics — and consumes ~1% of global energy.

questions.prompt: Modern chemistry has recovered some of alchemy's holism. Example:
options: Emergent properties (catalysis, self-assembly, phase transitions) cannot be reduced to atoms in isolation
questions.correctAnswer: Emergent properties (catalysis, self-assembly, phase transitions) cannot be reduced to atoms in isolation
questions.explanation: Catalytic surfaces, supramolecular assembly, molecular recognition, and phase transitions are explained by atoms plus interactions, but the patterns are not visible at the single-atom level. Alchemy was wrong about substance, right that 'the whole' matters. Reductionism plus emergence in tension.

title: Mind & Matter
description: Neurons, qualia, determinism, and consciousness — where biology, physics, and philosophy collide.

questions.prompt: A neuron fires when:
options: Electrons flow through it like a wire
Membrane voltage crosses threshold and Na+ channels open in cascade (action potential)
It is purely chemical, no electrical events
questions.correctAnswer: Membrane voltage crosses threshold and Na+ channels open in cascade (action potential)
questions.explanation: Resting ~ -70 mV; threshold ~ -55 mV; Na+ rushes in to ~ +30 mV; K+ exits to repolarize. Self-propagating wave down the axon. The nervous system is electrochemical, not a pure electric circuit.

questions.prompt: Leibniz's 'mill argument' (1714) anticipated which modern problem?
options: The explanatory gap: walking through the brain like a giant mill, we'd see mechanism but not perception itself
questions.correctAnswer: The explanatory gap: walking through the brain like a giant mill, we'd see mechanism but not perception itself
questions.explanation: Leibniz: imagine the brain enlarged to a mill; you would see parts pushing parts but never find perception. Modern: David Chalmers' 'hard problem' of consciousness. Why is there subjective experience at all? Open question in philosophy of mind.

questions.prompt: Determinism (Laplace's demon) says the future is fixed by present state plus laws. The strongest physics challenge is:
options: Quantum mechanics is fundamentally probabilistic (per the standard interpretation)
questions.correctAnswer: Quantum mechanics is fundamentally probabilistic (per the standard interpretation)
questions.explanation: Born rule: outcomes have probabilities, not certainties. Chaos amplifies tiny uncertainties — including quantum ones. Standard interpretation: indeterminism is real. Many-Worlds preserves determinism at the cost of branching reality. Free-will debate sometimes invokes this.

questions.prompt: The 'binding problem' in neuroscience asks:
options: How distributed brain activity (color, motion, shape, location) integrates into one unified percept
questions.correctAnswer: How distributed brain activity (color, motion, shape, location) integrates into one unified percept
questions.explanation: Visual cortex has separate areas for color (V4), motion (V5), shape, depth. Yet you see one cup, not features in pieces. Proposed solutions: synchrony (40 Hz gamma oscillations), attention, global workspace. Connects cellular biology to phenomenology.

questions.prompt: Penrose-Hameroff propose consciousness involves quantum effects in microtubules. Mainstream criticism:
options: The brain is too warm and wet — quantum coherence decoheres in ~10^-20 s, far too fast
questions.correctAnswer: The brain is too warm and wet — quantum coherence decoheres in ~10^-20 s, far too fast
questions.explanation: Tegmark's calculation: thermal noise destroys quantum coherence vastly faster than neural timescales (ms). Most neuroscientists view this as fatal. Defenders propose specific protected configurations. Open but uphill.

questions.prompt: Functionalism in philosophy of mind says:
options: Only carbon brains can have minds
A mental state is defined by its functional role; any substrate that implements the role realizes the state
questions.correctAnswer: A mental state is defined by its functional role; any substrate that implements the role realizes the state
questions.explanation: Putnam's idea: pain is not particular tissue, it's a role (tissue damage signal -> withdrawal + complaint). If silicon plays the same role, it could feel pain. Foundation of strong AI claims. Critics: Searle's Chinese Room; missing qualia.

questions.prompt: Libet's experiments (1980s) showed:
options: Brain activity (readiness potential) precedes the conscious decision to move by ~300 ms
Consciousness is faster than the brain
questions.correctAnswer: Brain activity (readiness potential) precedes the conscious decision to move by ~300 ms
questions.explanation: EEG signal in motor planning areas predicts choice before the subject reports deciding. Some interpret this as eliminating free will, others as showing only that conscious 'veto' matters. Methodological critiques exist (introspective timing).

questions.prompt: The 'knowledge argument' (Mary's room): Mary knows everything physical about color but lives in B&W. When she sees red, does she learn something new?
options: If yes, then there are non-physical facts about experience — a challenge for physicalism
questions.correctAnswer: If yes, then there are non-physical facts about experience — a challenge for physicalism
questions.explanation: Frank Jackson's thought experiment. Strong physicalists say she gains a new ability or representation, not a new fact. Property dualists say qualia are extra. Among the most discussed arguments in philosophy of mind.

questions.prompt: Anesthetics work but their consciousness-loss mechanism is not fully understood. A leading hypothesis:
options: Disrupted long-range cortical integration — consciousness fragments
questions.correctAnswer: Disrupted long-range cortical integration — consciousness fragments
questions.explanation: Drugs target diverse molecular receptors but converge on disrupting global communication between brain regions. Integrated Information Theory (Tononi) predicts this — consciousness needs integration. fMRI/EEG support. Practical clinical importance.

questions.prompt: If a perfect computer simulation of your brain were running, would it be conscious?
options: Depends on whether functional organization suffices for consciousness — central open question
questions.correctAnswer: Depends on whether functional organization suffices for consciousness — central open question
questions.explanation: Functionalists say yes; biological naturalists (Searle) say no — silicon lacks the right causal powers. IIT says it depends on the integration structure of the substrate. Ethical stakes if AI ever reaches that point.

title: Decipherment
description: Rosetta, Linear B, cuneiform, Maya glyphs — how lost scripts surrendered to combinatorics, statistics, and linguistic insight.

questions.prompt: The Rosetta Stone (1799) was crucial because it had:
options: The same decree in Greek + Egyptian hieroglyphics + Egyptian Demotic
questions.correctAnswer: The same decree in Greek + Egyptian hieroglyphics + Egyptian Demotic
questions.explanation: Greek was known. Decoders had a parallel text. Champollion (1822) proved hieroglyphs encoded sounds, not just symbols, and matched Coptic phonology. Bilingual texts are the dream of every decipherer.

questions.prompt: Linear B was deciphered (Ventris 1952) by recognizing it encoded:
options: An early form of Greek, written syllabically
questions.correctAnswer: An early form of Greek, written syllabically
questions.explanation: Ventris assumed Cretan origin (wrong) but used statistical patterns — sign frequencies and combinations on tablets — to identify a syllabary. When values produced Greek words, the system fell open. Combinatorial reasoning plus linguistic intuition.

questions.prompt: Decipherers estimate writing-system type from sign count: alphabets ~20-40, syllabaries ~50-200, logographic thousands. The Indus script has ~400 signs, suggesting:
questions.correctAnswer: Probably logosyllabic, though unconfirmed
questions.explanation: Sign-inventory size narrows possibilities. Linear A has ~80 signs (syllabary). The Indus script ~400 signs suggests a mixed log-syllabic system, but the language is unknown and inscriptions are very short — decipherment remains open.

questions.prompt: Frequency analysis (Al-Kindi, 9th c) cracked substitution ciphers by:
options: Matching ciphertext letter frequencies to expected language frequencies
questions.correctAnswer: Matching ciphertext letter frequencies to expected language frequencies
questions.explanation: In English, 'e' ~ 12.7%, 't' ~ 9.1%. The cipher's most common letter likely encodes 'e'. This cracks monoalphabetic ciphers in minutes. Same statistical principle helps with unknown scripts when the language family is suspected.

questions.prompt: Etruscan can be READ phonetically but not UNDERSTOOD because:
options: It is a language isolate with no known relatives — no parallels for vocabulary
questions.correctAnswer: It is a language isolate with no known relatives — no parallels for vocabulary
questions.explanation: We can pronounce inscriptions but lack a linguistic anchor. Decipherment requires bilinguals, related languages, or extensive context. Contrast Linear B (was Greek) with Etruscan (still mostly opaque).

questions.prompt: Indus Valley script remains undeciphered partly because:
options: Short inscriptions (avg 5 signs) + no known bilingual + unknown underlying language
questions.correctAnswer: Short inscriptions (avg 5 signs) + no known bilingual + unknown underlying language
questions.explanation: Most 'texts' are seal stamps with a handful of signs — insufficient context for statistical pattern matching. The underlying language (Dravidian? Indo-Aryan? isolate?) is unknown. ~400 signs suggests logosyllabic but is unconfirmed.

questions.prompt: Cuneiform was deciphered partly via Old Persian inscriptions (Behistun) that were trilingual. The math-y trick:
options: Royal name patterns ('X, son of Y, king of kings') gave known structure that pinned down values
questions.correctAnswer: Royal name patterns ('X, son of Y, king of kings') gave known structure that pinned down values
questions.explanation: If you know 'Darius son of Hystaspes' appears, you can locate those names in cuneiform and assign sound values. Constraint propagation across the trilingual unlocked Babylonian and Akkadian. A network of cross-references.

questions.prompt: Maya glyphs were decoded mid-20th c after recognizing they were:
options: Logosyllabic, encoding Mayan languages still spoken today
questions.correctAnswer: Logosyllabic, encoding Mayan languages still spoken today
questions.explanation: Yuri Knorozov (1952) showed glyphs combined logograms and syllables, encoding a real spoken language (Yucatec, Ch'ol). Living descendants helped reconstruct phonology. Earlier scholars (Eric Thompson) had insisted glyphs were purely symbolic — slowing progress for decades.

questions.prompt: Modern AI decipherment attempts (e.g. on Linear A) typically use:
options: Trained models comparing distributions of unknown script to known languages
questions.correctAnswer: Trained models comparing distributions of unknown script to known languages
questions.explanation: Embedding sign sequences and matching against known languages. Limited success — Linear A is still largely opaque, possibly because the language is unknown and the corpus is small. A tool, not an oracle.

questions.prompt: The Voynich Manuscript resists decipherment because:
options: Unique script + statistical features unlike any known language + may be hoax or constructed language
questions.correctAnswer: Unique script + statistical features unlike any known language + may be hoax or constructed language
questions.explanation: Word lengths and letter distributions don't match natural languages well, but aren't pure gibberish either. Carbon-dated to ~1404-1438. Open question whether it's a cipher, a constructed language, glossolalia, or elaborate fraud.

title: Light, Eye, Color
description: Photons, photoreceptors, and the experience of redness — physics through biology and into philosophy of mind.

questions.prompt: The 'visible' light range (~400-700 nm) is called visible because:
options: It is the only EM radiation in existence
It's the range our cone photoreceptors detect — other species see different ranges
questions.correctAnswer: It's the range our cone photoreceptors detect — other species see different ranges
questions.explanation: Bees see UV; pit vipers sense IR; mantis shrimp have 12+ photoreceptor types. 'Visible' is a biological accident of human retinal chemistry, not a physical feature of light. Anchored in solar peak emission and atmospheric transparency.

questions.prompt: Newton's prism (1666) split white light into colors. He concluded:
options: White light is a mixture; the prism refracts different wavelengths by different amounts
questions.correctAnswer: White light is a mixture; the prism refracts different wavelengths by different amounts
questions.explanation: Recombining the spectrum gave white again. Demolished the idea that the prism added color. Refractive index depends on wavelength = dispersion. Connects optics to color perception. Model for analytic decomposition in science.

questions.prompt: Young's double-slit experiment (1801) showed:
options: Light makes interference patterns, demonstrating wave behavior
questions.correctAnswer: Light makes interference patterns, demonstrating wave behavior
questions.explanation: Coherent light through two slits creates alternating bright/dark bands. Particles cannot do this. Combined with Maxwell's EM waves, this was the dominant view by 1860. Then Einstein (1905) reintroduced photons — wave-particle duality.

questions.prompt: Human cones come in three types (S, M, L). This is why:
options: Color reproduction works with three primaries — most human color vision is trichromatic
questions.correctAnswer: Color reproduction works with three primaries — most human color vision is trichromatic
questions.explanation: S ~ 420 nm (blue), M ~ 530 (green), L ~ 560 (red). Brain compares ratios. RGB screens and RYB paint exploit this. Some women are tetrachromatic; many mammals are dichromatic.

questions.prompt: Object 'color' = wavelength reflected. But the experience of redness (qualia) is:
options: Just neuron firing, with no remaining puzzle
The philosophical 'hard problem' — why does any wavelength feel like anything?
questions.correctAnswer: The philosophical 'hard problem' — why does any wavelength feel like anything?
questions.explanation: Physics specifies wavelengths; biology specifies neural responses; what about felt redness? Functionalists, eliminativists, and property dualists disagree. Locke's 'secondary qualities' foreshadowed it.

questions.prompt: An 'inverted spectrum' thought experiment (your red = my green, behaviorally identical) tests whether:
options: Qualia are fixed by function — if invertibility is conceivable without behavioral difference, function alone doesn't fix experience
questions.correctAnswer: Qualia are fixed by function — if invertibility is conceivable without behavioral difference, function alone doesn't fix experience
questions.explanation: If two beings are indistinguishable by behavior or brain function, no public test can decide. Functionalism says identical function = identical experience (no inversion). Critics say we can't rule it out. Long-running anti-functionalist argument.

questions.prompt: Vision starts when a photon hits retinal (cis-retinal in the opsin protein). The molecular event:
options: Photon flips retinal from cis to trans isomer, triggering a GPCR cascade
questions.correctAnswer: Photon flips retinal from cis to trans isomer, triggering a GPCR cascade
questions.explanation: One absorbed photon -> conformational change -> activates transducin -> closes Na+ channels -> hyperpolarizes the cell. Single-photon detection. Opsins evolved 600+ Mya. Same chemistry across vertebrates and most invertebrates.

questions.prompt: Why is the sky blue?
options: Blue is the natural color of air
Rayleigh scattering — shorter wavelengths scatter more by air molecules
questions.correctAnswer: Rayleigh scattering — shorter wavelengths scatter more by air molecules
questions.explanation: Scattering ~ 1/lambda^4. Blue (~450 nm) scatters about 5x more than red (~700 nm). The Sun appears yellowish because blue is scattered out. Sunsets are red because the path through atmosphere is long, leaving red.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't evolution favor wider spectral sensitivity in human eyes?
options: Tradeoffs: wider range loses spectral discrimination; UV damages tissue; IR is mostly thermal noise
questions.correctAnswer: Tradeoffs: wider range loses spectral discrimination; UV damages tissue; IR is mostly thermal noise
questions.explanation: The lens absorbs UV (some birds and insects see UV via different lenses). IR detection requires cooling or large apertures (snake pit organs are specialized). Human range is a compromise between resolution and information.

questions.prompt: Goethe rejected Newton's color theory and proposed color arises from the interplay of light and dark. Modern view:
options: Newton was right about light's physics; Goethe's psychology of color (afterimages, contrast) was a forerunner of perceptual science
questions.correctAnswer: Newton was right about light's physics; Goethe's psychology of color (afterimages, contrast) was a forerunner of perceptual science
questions.explanation: Goethe's experiments on simultaneous contrast, afterimages, and color preferences anticipated later vision science. Color is not only wavelength — it's wavelength + context + adaptation. Two truths: physical light vs. perceived color.

title: Cathedrals & Stress
description: Arches, domes, and flying buttresses — how stone, geometry, and physics built the largest spaces of the pre-industrial world.

questions.prompt: Roman and Romanesque architecture leaned on round arches. The load behavior:
options: Thrust outward — heavy walls and buttresses absorb the horizontal force
questions.correctAnswer: Thrust outward — heavy walls and buttresses absorb the horizontal force
questions.explanation: An arch converts vertical load into a mix of vertical and horizontal compression. Stone is ~10x stronger in compression than in tension, so arches let stone span. Outward thrust must be contained, hence thick walls and small windows.

questions.prompt: Gothic architecture (12th c onward) added pointed arches and flying buttresses, with the effect that:
options: Thrust was redirected to external supports, allowing thinner walls and huge windows
questions.correctAnswer: Thrust was redirected to external supports, allowing thinner walls and huge windows
questions.explanation: The pointed arch reduces lateral thrust per unit height. Flying buttresses transfer remaining thrust over the side aisles to massive piers. Wall load is relieved, leaving space for stained glass. Engineering enabled the visual revolution.

questions.prompt: Stone has high compressive but low tensile strength. The most common cause of historical cathedral collapse:
options: Tension in unintended places (settling, wind, vault thrust) producing cracks then failure
questions.correctAnswer: Tension in unintended places (settling, wind, vault thrust) producing cracks then failure
questions.explanation: Beauvais (1284) collapsed because piers could not carry concentrated loads. Differential settlement induces tension. Builders learned heuristically — failures led to refinements. Modern finite-element analysis confirms their geometric intuitions.

questions.prompt: The Pantheon dome (~125 CE) is unreinforced concrete. Romans kept it up by:
options: Grading the aggregate — heavy basalt at the bottom, light pumice at the top
questions.correctAnswer: Grading the aggregate — heavy basalt at the bottom, light pumice at the top
questions.explanation: The density gradient cuts upper-dome weight by ~30%. Coffers further reduce mass without weakening structure. Diameter (43.3 m) was unmatched until Brunelleschi's Florence dome (1436) — using a different ingenious technique (double shell, herringbone bricks).

questions.prompt: Why are cathedral spires often near the structural limit of stone?
options: Scaling laws — strength scales with cross-section area while weight scales with volume
questions.correctAnswer: Scaling laws — strength scales with cross-section area while weight scales with volume
questions.explanation: Galileo's insight (1638). Self-weight stress grows with size. Stone's compressive strength of ~50-100 MPa caps tower height to a few hundred meters. Same reason mountains cannot exceed ~10 km on Earth.

questions.prompt: The shape of a hanging chain (catenary) inverted gives the optimal arch shape because:
options: A chain in tension carries only axial loads; inverting puts pure compression along the axis with no bending
questions.correctAnswer: A chain in tension carries only axial loads; inverting puts pure compression along the axis with no bending
questions.explanation: Hooke's hint to Wren (1675); Gaudi built on it. A catenary self-supports under its own weight without bending moments. Inverted, all stress is compression. Sagrada Familia's columns and St Paul's dome use this principle.

questions.prompt: Ancient lime mortar vs. modern Portland cement — the key behavioral difference:
options: Lime mortar deforms slightly and self-heals via dissolution-reprecipitation of CaCO3; Portland cracks brittle and irreversibly
questions.correctAnswer: Lime mortar deforms slightly and self-heals via dissolution-reprecipitation of CaCO3; Portland cracks brittle and irreversibly
questions.explanation: Lime's flexibility tolerates settling; cracks reseal as atmospheric CO2 converts Ca(OH)2 to CaCO3. Portland cement is stiffer and stronger short-term but cracks are permanent. Restoration projects often must use lime to match historic behavior.

questions.prompt: Reinforced concrete combines steel's tensile strength with concrete's compressive strength. Why does it work despite the materials being so different?
options: Matched thermal expansion coefficients + chemical bonding + alkaline concrete passivates steel against rust
questions.correctAnswer: Matched thermal expansion coefficients + chemical bonding + alkaline concrete passivates steel against rust
questions.explanation: Both expand at ~12 um/m/C, so joint expansion. Alkaline concrete passivates steel. Concrete (compression) plus steel rebar (tension) covers both load types. A 19th-century invention enabling modern skyscrapers, bridges, and dams.

questions.prompt: Earthquakes apply lateral cyclic loads. Modern buildings survive them by:
options: Ductile design — deforming inelastically without collapsing, dissipating energy
questions.correctAnswer: Ductile design — deforming inelastically without collapsing, dissipating energy
questions.explanation: Steel frames and properly detailed reinforced concrete yield plastically. Energy goes into deformation, not catastrophic failure. Old masonry cathedrals are brittle; many in seismic zones cracked or collapsed (Assisi 1997, L'Aquila 2009).

questions.prompt: The transition from Gothic to Renaissance domes (Brunelleschi's Florence, 1436) required:
options: Solving how to build a 42 m dome without wooden centering — herringbone brickwork plus horizontal tension chains
questions.correctAnswer: Solving how to build a 42 m dome without wooden centering — herringbone brickwork plus horizontal tension chains
questions.explanation: Wood centering would have required a forest. Brunelleschi designed a self-supporting double shell with bricks laid in herringbone pattern — each course locked by the next. Iron and stone rings absorb hoop tension. Rediscovered Roman techniques and invented new ones, sparking Renaissance engineering ambition.

title: Codes & Ciphers
description: Caesar to RSA — number theory, computer science, and the wars decided by broken codes.

questions.prompt: RSA's security rests on which mathematical asymmetry?
options: Multiplying two large primes is easy; factoring their product is hard
Adding two large primes is hard but multiplication is easy
Large primes are easy to find but small ones are hard
Modular exponentiation is reversible only with a quantum computer
questions.correctAnswer: Multiplying two large primes is easy; factoring their product is hard
questions.explanation: RSA exploits the gap between trapdoor multiplication and integer factorisation. Shor's algorithm closes this gap on a quantum computer, which is why post-quantum cryptography is being standardised.

questions.prompt: The Vigenère cipher resisted casual attack for centuries. What broke it?
options: Kasiski's method: spotting repeated ciphertext segments to deduce key length, then frequency analysis on each subkey
questions.correctAnswer: Kasiski's method: spotting repeated ciphertext segments to deduce key length, then frequency analysis on each subkey
questions.explanation: Once you know the key length k, the Vigenère collapses into k independent Caesar ciphers — each solvable by letter-frequency analysis. Babbage discovered this earlier but did not publish.

questions.prompt: Bletchley Park's break of Enigma exploited the fact that no Enigma rotor would ever encrypt a letter to itself.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: This self-non-mapping was a design flaw. It let cribs (guessed plaintext like 'WETTERBERICHT') be aligned against ciphertext by ruling out positions where any letter mapped to itself, drastically pruning the bombe's search.

questions.prompt: Diffie-Hellman key exchange relies on the hardness of computing the ____ in a finite cyclic group — the inverse problem of fast modular exponentiation.
questions.correctAnswer: discrete logarithm
questions.explanation: Both parties exchange g^a and g^b mod p; recovering a or b from g^a requires solving the discrete log, believed hard in suitable groups but again broken by Shor's algorithm.

questions.prompt: Match each cipher / system to the underlying mathematical object it abuses.

pairs.right: Modular addition mod 26
Hardness of integer factorisation
Discrete log on an elliptic curve group
Information-theoretic XOR with truly random key

questions.explanation: Each cryptosystem rests on a hard problem (factoring, discrete log) or an information-theoretic guarantee (one-time pad). Choice of group matters: ECC achieves equivalent security with much smaller keys than RSA.

questions.prompt: Why did the Allies' Enigma break remain classified until the 1970s, despite ending in 1945?
options: The decryption methods were embarrassingly simple
Many Axis-pattern Enigma machines were sold to post-war states; revealing the break would warn them their traffic was readable
Britain feared the USSR would retaliate against Bletchley staff
Turing's homosexuality made the project politically toxic
questions.correctAnswer: Many Axis-pattern Enigma machines were sold to post-war states; revealing the break would warn them their traffic was readable
questions.explanation: Captured Enigmas and Lorenz machines were re-distributed to Commonwealth and other governments. Keeping ULTRA secret meant Britain could keep reading their cables. Disclosed only when those systems were retired.

title: Symmetry
description: Group theory underwrites particle physics and crystal classes — and Noether ties symmetry to conservation.

questions.prompt: Noether's theorem links continuous symmetries to conservation laws. Which pair is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: Time translation ↔ energy conservation
questions.explanation: Time-translation symmetry yields energy conservation; space-translation yields momentum; rotational symmetry yields angular momentum. Internal U(1) gauge symmetry of QED yields electric charge conservation.

questions.prompt: Crystals are classified into exactly ____ point groups (crystallographic classes) by combining the allowed rotation axes (1, 2, 3, 4, 6) with mirror and inversion symmetries.
questions.explanation: The crystallographic restriction theorem forbids 5-fold and >6-fold rotation axes in periodic 3D lattices, leaving 32 possible point groups. (Quasicrystals break periodicity to admit 5-fold symmetry — Shechtman, 2011 Nobel.)

questions.prompt: The Standard Model's gauge group is SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1). Each factor corresponds to which interaction?
options: Strong, electromagnetic, hypercharge (mixed at low energy into weak + EM)
questions.correctAnswer: Strong, electromagnetic, hypercharge (mixed at low energy into weak + EM)
questions.explanation: SU(3) is colour (QCD); SU(2) and U(1) describe weak isospin and hypercharge — the Higgs mechanism breaks them down to the unbroken U(1) of electromagnetism, with the weak force mediated by the now-massive W and Z bosons.

questions.prompt: Chirality (handedness) appears in molecules, crystals, AND the weak interaction — which couples only to left-handed fermions.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Wu's 1957 experiment showed cobalt-60 betas emit preferentially against the nuclear spin: parity is violated. The weak force discriminates handedness in a way the strong, EM, and gravity do not.

questions.prompt: Match each symmetry operation to where it appears.

pairs.right: Wallpaper / space groups
CPT theorem
Centrosymmetric crystals (e.g., NaCl)
Angular-momentum conservation

questions.explanation: Discrete symmetries (glide, inversion) live in crystals; continuous ones (translations, rotations, gauge) generate conservation laws via Noether. CPT (the product) is the deepest discrete symmetry of relativistic QFT.

questions.prompt: Why are 5-fold rotational axes forbidden in ordinary 3D crystal lattices?
options: Pentagons cannot tile the plane without gaps or overlaps; periodic 3D lattices inherit this restriction
Five is a prime number, which interferes with translational symmetry
questions.correctAnswer: Pentagons cannot tile the plane without gaps or overlaps; periodic 3D lattices inherit this restriction
questions.explanation: The crystallographic restriction theorem follows from demanding that translation by a lattice vector commutes with the rotation. Quasicrystals — aperiodic but ordered — sidestep periodicity and DO exhibit 5-fold patterns.

title: Mathematics of Music
description: Pythagorean ratios, Fourier decomposition, and the irrational compromise of equal temperament.

questions.prompt: An octave is a frequency ratio of 2:1. A perfect fifth is approximately what ratio?
questions.explanation: Pythagorean tuning derives intervals from 3:2 (fifth) and 2:1 (octave). 5:4 is the major third (just intonation), 9:8 a major tone, 16:15 a diatonic semitone.

questions.prompt: Equal temperament divides the octave into 12 equal semitones. Each semitone is a frequency ratio of the ____ root of 2.
questions.correctAnswer: 12th
questions.explanation: 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.0595. This makes every key sound equally (slightly) out of tune — the price for being able to modulate freely. Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier celebrated this compromise.

questions.prompt: Why does a violin and a clarinet playing the same note sound different (different timbre)?
options: They produce the same fundamental but different relative amplitudes of harmonic partials (Fourier spectrum)
Air resistance damps high frequencies for woodwinds only
The brain assigns timbre at random
questions.correctAnswer: They produce the same fundamental but different relative amplitudes of harmonic partials (Fourier spectrum)
questions.explanation: Timbre is the harmonic spectrum: which overtones above the fundamental are present and how loud. Fourier analysis decomposes the waveform into these partials. A clarinet emphasises odd harmonics (closed-cylindrical bore); a violin contains a richer mix.

questions.prompt: The Pythagorean comma is the small frequency mismatch you accumulate by stacking 12 perfect fifths versus 7 octaves — about 23.5 cents.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Stacking fifths gives (3/2)^12 ≈ 129.75; stacking 7 octaves gives 2^7 = 128. The ratio 129.75/128 ≈ 1.0136 (~23.5 cents) is the comma. Equal temperament smears it across all 12 fifths.

questions.prompt: Match each acoustical phenomenon to its mathematical / physical cause.

pairs.right: Linear interference between close frequencies

pairs.left: Resonance peaks in a violin body
pairs.right: Eigenmodes of a coupled mechanical system
Nonlinear distortion in the ear / instrument

pairs.left: Doppler shift of a passing siren
pairs.right: Source motion relative to the observer

questions.explanation: Western music theory sits on top of physics: linear superposition for beats, eigenvalue problems for resonance, and nonlinearity for combination tones audible only inside the cochlea.

questions.prompt: Why did Pythagoreans treat consonance and small-integer ratios as a metaphysical truth — and what did Western music gradually abandon?
options: They believed the cosmos itself was numerical (musica universalis); equal temperament abandoned exact integer ratios for modulation across all keys
They believed only divine instruments could play in tune; modern music abandoned divinity
They thought irrational numbers did not exist; modern music abandoned counterpoint
They believed timbre encoded virtue; modern music abandoned timbre
questions.correctAnswer: They believed the cosmos itself was numerical (musica universalis); equal temperament abandoned exact integer ratios for modulation across all keys
questions.explanation: Pythagorean cosmology saw the planets producing inaudible harmonies in integer ratios. The shift to equal temperament — needed for keyboard polyphony — replaced exact ratios with the irrational 2^(1/12), severing music's claim to numerical purity.

title: Networks Everywhere
description: Graphs describe food webs, the internet, and social ties — and their structure dictates resilience.

questions.prompt: A 'scale-free' network has a degree distribution that follows what?
questions.correctAnswer: Power law (P(k) ~ k^-γ)
questions.explanation: Scale-free networks (web links, citation graphs, some protein interactions) have hubs of all sizes — no characteristic scale. Erdős–Rényi random graphs by contrast give a Poisson degree distribution with a characteristic mean.

questions.prompt: Scale-free networks are robust against random node failure but fragile to targeted attacks on hubs.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Random failures usually hit low-degree nodes (most nodes are low-degree). Removing the few high-degree hubs shatters the network. The internet's autonomous-system graph and ecological food webs share this vulnerability.

questions.prompt: Königsberg's seven bridges: Euler showed no walk crosses each bridge exactly once. Why?
options: More than two vertices had odd degree
questions.correctAnswer: More than two vertices had odd degree
questions.explanation: An Eulerian path exists iff the graph has exactly 0 or 2 odd-degree vertices. Königsberg had four. This 1736 paper founded graph theory.

questions.prompt: The 'six degrees of separation' result — Milgram's experiment and later studies — is an empirical instance of the ____-____ network property: high clustering plus short average path length.
questions.correctAnswer: small-world
questions.explanation: Watts and Strogatz (1998) showed that adding a few long-range 'shortcut' edges to a regular lattice collapses path lengths from O(n) to O(log n) while preserving local clustering. Many real networks live in this regime.

questions.prompt: Match each real-world network to its dominant topology / property.

pairs.right: Scale-free with hub backbones

pairs.left: Food web in a coral reef
pairs.right: Modular, often nested, with keystone species
Small-world with hub-rich 'rich club'
Self-organising, near-optimal transport network

questions.explanation: Across kingdoms, networks converge on a handful of motifs — small-world clustering, scale-free hubs, modular community structure — because these solve recurring problems of efficient transport and resilience.

questions.prompt: Removing a 'keystone species' (a top predator, say) from a food web often collapses richness. What graph-theoretic property is being lost?
options: Top-down regulation of trophic cascades — a few high-betweenness nodes prevent runaway dominance by mid-trophic species
questions.correctAnswer: Top-down regulation of trophic cascades — a few high-betweenness nodes prevent runaway dominance by mid-trophic species
questions.explanation: Sea otters control urchins; wolves control elk; sharks control mid-level predators. Their high betweenness centrality means many short paths run through them. Lose them and lower trophic levels overgraze, collapsing kelp/coral/grass primary producers.

title: Heat & Empire
description: Steam engines, the Carnot limit, and how thermodynamics rewrote the 19th century.

questions.prompt: The Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot tells us what about real heat engines?
options: They can reach 100% with the right design
There is a hard upper bound set only by the reservoir temperatures, regardless of working fluid
questions.correctAnswer: There is a hard upper bound set only by the reservoir temperatures, regardless of working fluid
questions.explanation: Carnot's 1824 result was the first hint of the second law: no engine running between two reservoirs can exceed this. Real engines lose more to friction, irreversibility, and finite-time operation.

questions.prompt: Watt's separate condenser massively improved on Newcomen's atmospheric engine by avoiding repeatedly cooling and reheating the working cylinder.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Newcomen's design wasted ~99% of heat by condensing steam inside the main cylinder, then reheating the iron walls each stroke. Watt's separate condenser kept the cylinder hot — a thermodynamic insight that cut coal use by ~75% and made the engine economic far from coalfields.

questions.prompt: Why was Britain's transition from charcoal to coke (coal-derived) for iron smelting so consequential?
options: Coke is sulphur-free and produces purer iron than charcoal
Britain was deforesting; coke decoupled iron output from forest area, enabling massive scale
questions.correctAnswer: Britain was deforesting; coke decoupled iron output from forest area, enabling massive scale
questions.explanation: Abraham Darby's 1709 coke smelting at Coalbrookdale unhitched iron from the slow-growing forest. Combined with steam-pumped mines, steam-driven blast, and rail transport, this is the classical 'energy transition' to fossil fuels.

questions.prompt: The second law of thermodynamics is often summarised by the inequality: in any spontaneous process, the total ____ of an isolated system never decreases.
questions.correctAnswer: entropy
questions.explanation: Clausius (1865): 'Die Entropie der Welt strebt einem Maximum zu.' Boltzmann later gave the statistical interpretation S = k log W. Heat engines must dump entropy to a cold reservoir, capping their efficiency.

questions.prompt: Match each technical advance to the bottleneck it broke.

pairs.right: Cheap mass production of mild steel
Compact engines small enough for locomotives
Loads & speeds heavier than cast iron could bear
Repair without bespoke craftsmen

questions.explanation: Industrialisation was a stack: thermodynamic theory at the top, but underneath sat metallurgy, machine tooling, and logistics. Removing any layer collapsed the whole.

questions.prompt: Why does steel fatigue under cyclic loading even when peak stress stays below the static yield?
options: Repeated stress nucleates and grows microcracks at slip-band intrusions/extrusions
questions.correctAnswer: Repeated stress nucleates and grows microcracks at slip-band intrusions/extrusions
questions.explanation: Cyclic plastic strain at a microscopic level builds slip bands; intrusions create stress risers that initiate fatigue cracks. Comet jet airliner crashes (1954) made fatigue failure painfully famous and changed pressure-cabin design.

title: Origins of Life
description: Prebiotic chemistry, RNA worlds, hydrothermal vents — where chemistry crosses into biology.

questions.prompt: The Miller-Urey experiment (1953) showed what?
options: That life arose in a single step
That amino acids form abiotically when energy is added to a reducing-atmosphere mixture of CH4, NH3, H2O, H2
That RNA is the original genetic material
questions.correctAnswer: That amino acids form abiotically when energy is added to a reducing-atmosphere mixture of CH4, NH3, H2O, H2
questions.explanation: Sparking a flask with a then-presumed early-Earth atmosphere produced glycine, alanine, and other amino acids. Modern atmospheric models doubt the strongly reducing mixture, but the experiment proved abiotic synthesis is chemically easy.

questions.prompt: The 'RNA world' hypothesis proposes that RNA preceded both DNA and proteins because RNA can both store information and catalyse reactions (ribozymes).
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Discovery of catalytic RNA (Cech, Altman, 1980s Nobel) made the RNA world plausible. The ribosome's catalytic core is itself a ribozyme — molecular fossil evidence for the hypothesis.

questions.prompt: Why are alkaline hydrothermal vents (e.g., Lost City) considered a strong candidate for life's origin?
options: Their porous serpentinite chimneys provide natural proton gradients across thin mineral membranes — abiotic chemiosmosis
questions.correctAnswer: Their porous serpentinite chimneys provide natural proton gradients across thin mineral membranes — abiotic chemiosmosis
questions.explanation: All life uses proton gradients across membranes for energy (Mitchell, Nobel 1978). Lost City vents naturally provide this gradient — alkaline vent fluid against acidic ocean — without enzymes. Lane and Martin's 'free-energy' hypothesis builds on this.

questions.prompt: LUCA — the Last Universal Common Ancestor — sits at the root of the tree of life and is inferred to have already used the genetic code, ribosomes, and ____ for energy storage. (Three-letter abbreviation.)
questions.correctAnswer: ATP
questions.explanation: Adenosine triphosphate is universal across all three domains (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya), making it overwhelmingly likely that LUCA already used it. The deep universality is one of the strongest single arguments for monophyletic origin of life.

questions.prompt: Match each candidate prebiotic environment to its proposed advantage.

pairs.right: Concentration via wet/dry cycles
Natural proton gradients in mineral membranes
Mineral templates organising organic monomers
Reducing chemistry concentrated by impact heating

questions.explanation: No consensus exists. Each environment solves a piece of the puzzle: concentration, gradient, templating, or chemistry. The truth may have required multiple environments coupled.

questions.prompt: Why is the homochirality of biology (all amino acids L, all sugars D) a deep puzzle?
options: Chirality breaks parity, which physics says is conserved
Abiotic syntheses produce racemic (50/50) mixtures; some symmetry-breaking mechanism had to amplify a tiny initial bias
questions.correctAnswer: Abiotic syntheses produce racemic (50/50) mixtures; some symmetry-breaking mechanism had to amplify a tiny initial bias
questions.explanation: Frank-style autocatalytic models can amplify ppm-level chiral excess to homochirality. Candidate biases include circularly polarised UV from neutron stars, parity violation in beta decay, or chiral mineral surfaces. Meteoritic amino acids show modest L-excesses, consistent with extraterrestrial seeding.

title: Drugs & the Brain
description: Receptors, blood-brain barriers, and the philosophical mess of altering subjective experience.

questions.prompt: An 'agonist' at a receptor does what?
options: Blocks the receptor without activating it
Binds and triggers the receptor's signalling response
questions.correctAnswer: Binds and triggers the receptor's signalling response
questions.explanation: Antagonists block without activating; partial agonists give submaximal response; inverse agonists actively suppress baseline activity. The agonist/antagonist distinction is foundational to pharmacology.

questions.prompt: Why must a CNS drug usually be small and somewhat lipophilic?
options: So it dissolves in the stomach
To cross the blood-brain barrier — tight junctions of brain capillary endothelium exclude large or hydrophilic molecules
To avoid being filtered by the kidneys
questions.correctAnswer: To cross the blood-brain barrier — tight junctions of brain capillary endothelium exclude large or hydrophilic molecules
questions.explanation: The BBB is selective: small lipid-soluble molecules cross by diffusion, others need active transporters. Drug design for neurology constantly fights this barrier; many promising leads die in BBB-permeability optimisation.

questions.prompt: Classical psychedelics (LSD, psilocin, DMT) all act primarily as agonists at the 5-HT2A serotonin receptor.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: 5-HT2A agonism is the shared pharmacological signature; antagonists (ketanserin) block subjective effects. The downstream cortical disorganisation (reduced top-down predictive control) is currently the leading neural-correlates account.

questions.prompt: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) work by blocking the ____, raising synaptic serotonin levels.
questions.correctAnswer: serotonin transporter
questions.explanation: SERT (the SLC6A4 transporter) reabsorbs serotonin from the synapse. Blocking it lifts synaptic 5-HT. Therapeutic effect typically lags onset of SERT inhibition by weeks, hinting that downstream receptor adaptations — not raw serotonin — drive mood change.

questions.prompt: Match each substance to its primary pharmacological mechanism.

pairs.right: Adenosine A1/A2A receptor antagonist
μ-opioid receptor agonist
Dopamine reuptake inhibitor
GABA-A positive allosteric modulator

questions.explanation: Different drugs hit completely different molecular targets to converge on overlapping behavioural effects (sedation, euphoria, stimulation). 'Mechanism of action' often does not predict subjective phenomenology.

questions.prompt: If general anaesthesia abolishes consciousness while preserving most brain activity, what does this suggest for theories of mind?
options: Specific patterns of integrated activity (not just any activity) are required — sympathetic to integrated information / global workspace theories
There is no neural correlate of consciousness
questions.correctAnswer: Specific patterns of integrated activity (not just any activity) are required — sympathetic to integrated information / global workspace theories
questions.explanation: Anaesthetics like propofol disrupt long-range cortical integration while preserving local activity. Both Tononi's IIT and Dehaene's global workspace predict this loss-of-integration signature. This is one of the few empirical handles on the hard problem.

title: Volcanoes & Extinctions
description: Flood basalts, iridium layers, and the punctuations that reset evolution.

questions.prompt: The end-Permian extinction (~252 Ma) killed ~96% of marine species. The leading cause is now considered to be:
options: A bolide impact larger than Chicxulub
Eruption of the Siberian Traps — flood basalts triggering ocean anoxia, acidification, and CO2-driven warming
questions.correctAnswer: Eruption of the Siberian Traps — flood basalts triggering ocean anoxia, acidification, and CO2-driven warming
questions.explanation: Millions of km^3 of basalt erupted over ~1 Myr, releasing CO2, SO2, halogens, and ignited coal seams. The cascade — warming, anoxia, low ocean pH, methane release — explains the marine devastation.

questions.prompt: The K-Pg boundary's worldwide iridium spike was Alvarez & Alvarez's key evidence for a meteorite impact.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Iridium is rare in Earth's crust but abundant in chondritic asteroids. The 1980 paper proposed a ~10 km bolide; Chicxulub crater (1990) confirmed it. The Deccan Traps were also erupting — debate continues over their relative contribution.

questions.prompt: Why does ocean acidification preferentially harm calcifying organisms (corals, foraminifera, pteropods)?
options: Lower pH dissolves carbonate skeletons and lowers carbonate-ion availability for shell building
Acid kills all marine life equally
questions.correctAnswer: Lower pH dissolves carbonate skeletons and lowers carbonate-ion availability for shell building
questions.explanation: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3-, lowering CO3^2- and the saturation state Ω of aragonite/calcite. Below Ω = 1 shells dissolve. End-Permian and PETM both show selective loss of calcifiers.

questions.prompt: The K-Pg impact's site is the ~180 km buried ____ crater on the Yucatán Peninsula. (One word.)
questions.correctAnswer: Chicxulub
questions.explanation: Found via gravity and magnetic anomalies in Pemex oil-survey data. Drilling the peak ring (Expedition 364, 2016) recovered impact-shocked granite and confirmed the Cretaceous–Paleogene timing.

questions.prompt: Match each mass extinction to its leading proximal cause.

pairs.right: Glaciation, sea-level fall, and possible gamma-ray burst
Anoxic ocean events, possibly with land-plant feedbacks
Siberian Traps flood basalts → warming + anoxia
Chicxulub impact (and Deccan Traps contribution)

questions.explanation: The 'Big Five' have heterogeneous causes — impacts, basalt provinces, glaciation, anoxia. The recurring theme is rapid environmental change outpacing adaptation, especially for slow-evolving large taxa.

questions.prompt: Why do mass extinctions sometimes trigger evolutionary radiations?
options: They eliminate dominant taxa, freeing ecological niches that surviving lineages rapidly diversify into
They make natural selection stop working
questions.correctAnswer: They eliminate dominant taxa, freeing ecological niches that surviving lineages rapidly diversify into
questions.explanation: The K-Pg removed non-avian dinosaurs; mammals (small, opportunistic) radiated within ~10 Myr into rodents, primates, ungulates, whales. The end-Permian opened the way for archosaurs, leading to dinosaurs themselves.

title: Chaos
description: Lorenz attractors, weather, fractals — when nonlinear dynamics defeats long-range prediction.

questions.prompt: What characterises a chaotic dynamical system?
options: Deterministic equations with sensitive dependence on initial conditions: trajectories diverge exponentially
Periodic motion with a long period
questions.correctAnswer: Deterministic equations with sensitive dependence on initial conditions: trajectories diverge exponentially
questions.explanation: Chaos is fully deterministic: same equations, same initial state, same outcome. The catch is that infinitesimally close initial states diverge exponentially fast (positive Lyapunov exponent), capping our practical prediction horizon.

questions.prompt: Edward Lorenz's 'butterfly effect' was discovered when he restarted a simulation from rounded printed-out numbers and got a totally different forecast.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: 1961, MIT. Lorenz had typed 0.506 instead of 0.506127; weeks of simulated weather diverged completely. The strange attractor he then characterised (the Lorenz attractor) became the icon of chaos.

questions.prompt: The Mandelbrot set's boundary has Hausdorff dimension exactly:
questions.correctAnswer: Between 1 and 2 (and equal to 2)
questions.explanation: Shishikura proved (1991) that the boundary has Hausdorff dimension 2 — maximally 'space-filling' for a curve. This is part of why fractals describe so much of the natural world's roughness (coastlines, lungs, river networks).

questions.prompt: In a chaotic system, the average exponential rate at which nearby trajectories separate is called the ____ exponent.
questions.correctAnswer: Lyapunov
questions.explanation: λ > 0 is the technical signature of chaos. The inverse 1/λ gives the predictability horizon: doubling forecast accuracy adds only a fixed time, not a multiplicative factor — fundamentally limiting weather prediction beyond ~2 weeks.

questions.prompt: Match each fluid / nonlinear phenomenon to its governing concept.

pairs.right: Energy cascade across a scale range with -5/3 spectrum
Feigenbaum constant δ ≈ 4.669
Balance of nonlinearity and dispersion
Bounded trajectories with fractal structure

questions.explanation: Nonlinear systems generate a small zoo of universal behaviours. Feigenbaum's constant is the same for any unimodal-map period-doubling route — a striking universality across very different physical systems.

questions.prompt: Why is reliable weather forecasting fundamentally limited to ~2 weeks?
options: Atmospheric dynamics are chaotic; tiny initial-condition errors double on a ~2-day timescale, swamping the forecast within ~10–14 days
Satellites cannot observe the upper atmosphere
questions.correctAnswer: Atmospheric dynamics are chaotic; tiny initial-condition errors double on a ~2-day timescale, swamping the forecast within ~10–14 days
questions.explanation: Even with a perfect model and dense observations, the positive Lyapunov exponent of the atmosphere caps deterministic prediction. Beyond that, only ensemble probabilistic forecasts make sense.

title: Genes & Languages
description: Comparative method meets phylogenetics — language families and human migrations move in parallel.

questions.prompt: Reconstruction of Proto-Indo-European relies on the ____ method: systematic sound correspondences across daughter languages.
questions.correctAnswer: Comparative method
questions.explanation: Pioneered by Bopp, Grimm, and the 19th-century philologists. Regular sound laws (e.g., Grimm's Law for Germanic) let scholars reconstruct lexicon and morphology of an unattested ancestor — exactly analogous to inferring ancestral DNA states.

questions.prompt: Cavalli-Sforza showed that genetic and linguistic family trees of human populations correlate strongly — though not perfectly.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: His 1988 paper aligned classical genetic markers with linguistic phyla. Mismatches (Hungarian-speaking Europeans cluster genetically with neighbours, not with Uralic populations) reveal language shifts without large-scale population replacement.

questions.prompt: Why is mtDNA particularly useful for tracing human migrations?
options: It mutates faster than nuclear DNA, doesn't recombine, and is inherited only from the mother — a clean female lineage
It is the only DNA with introns
questions.correctAnswer: It mutates faster than nuclear DNA, doesn't recombine, and is inherited only from the mother — a clean female lineage
questions.explanation: Y-chromosome (NRY) gives the analogous male line. Combined, they let us infer 'mitochondrial Eve' and 'Y-chromosomal Adam', and trace expansions like the out-of-Africa migration ~60 ka.

questions.prompt: The expansion of Bantu-speaking peoples across sub-Saharan Africa over the last ~3000 years shows a tight correlation between language spread and movement of ____ — a genetic signature alongside agricultural and ironworking technologies.
questions.correctAnswer: people
questions.explanation: Bantu expansion is one of the cleanest examples of demic diffusion: people, languages, crops (yams, sorghum), and iron metallurgy spread together from a Cameroon-area homeland. Contrast with later language shifts where genes barely moved.

questions.prompt: Match each language family to a key associated migration / homeland hypothesis.

pairs.right: Steppe (Yamnaya) hypothesis ~5000 BP
Out of Taiwan, ~5000 BP, across Pacific
Cameroon-Nigeria borderland, ~3000 BP
West-Siberian / Volga-Ural origin, late Holocene

questions.explanation: Each family pairs a linguistic phylogeny with archaeological + genetic evidence. Yamnaya ancient-DNA studies (2015) gave Indo-European new biological footing; Austronesian's Pacific spread is one of the most extensive in human prehistory.

questions.prompt: Why must one be cautious mapping language families directly onto genetic clusters?
options: Languages can shift faster than genes — elite dominance, prestige, conquest, or trade can spread a language without large-scale population replacement
questions.correctAnswer: Languages can shift faster than genes — elite dominance, prestige, conquest, or trade can spread a language without large-scale population replacement
questions.explanation: Hungary speaks Uralic Hungarian but clusters genetically with Slavic neighbours; much of Latin America speaks Spanish/Portuguese without proportionate Iberian ancestry. Language spread modes (demic vs. cultural) make the gene/language map noisy.
